source.title: Pruning's Effect on Generalization Through the Lens of Training and Regularization
source.authors: Tian Jin; Michael Carbin; Daniel M. Roy; Jonathan Frankle; G. Dziugaite

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses overparameterization and cites double-descent work, but its experiments investigate pruning, training time, and width reduction—not whether test error follows the claimed double-descent curves or peaks at an interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The study reports test-error results from pruning and model-width sweeps, plus comparisons across training time. These bear on size and generalization, but it does not identify or test an interpolation threshold, or report a fall-rise-fall curve over model size, epochs, or sample size. The related results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites double-descent work (Nakkiran et al.; Belkin et al.) only to motivate its question about pruning in the over-parameterized regime. Its experiments compare pruning with extended dense training and with width down-scaling. It never locates an interpolation threshold. It reports no fall-rise-fall curve over model size, epochs or samples. It does not vary sample size or test regularization tuning against a peak. It neither tests nor relies on any version, so T6.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that size reduction does not fully explain pruning's generalization benefit. Pruning gives better training at some sparsities (from extended cyclic-LR training) and additional regularization at others (from size reduction, mitigating noisy examples). Which effect dominates at optimal sparsity depends on label noise, and both are needed.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses iterative magnitude pruning with learning-rate rewinding and compares it with extended dense training and width reduction; it does not reproduce the double-descent methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that outcomes vary with label-noise level, architecture and dataset, and with pruning choices including weight resetting and weight-selection heuristic.

fits_no_version.finding: With injected label noise, shrinking the width of standard dense CNNs (each model 80% the width of the previous) lowers test error over the tested range. This improvement is similar to pruning's, but no interpolation threshold is located.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under label noise, reducing the size of standard-width CNNs can improve test error via a regularization effect on noisy examples.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning to optimal sparsity beats the dense model on 11 of 13 noisy benchmarks and matches it on the rest. On clean data, extended cyclic-LR dense training matches pruning, so size reduction alone does not explain the gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning's generalization benefit decomposes into better training (from extended cyclic training) and size-reduction regularization (mainly under label noise).

record.problems: The evidence is empirical and limited to the reported image-classification benchmarks and pruning setups. Many size and training-time curves are presented in figures; the text does not provide numerical values for every point. The authors report three random-seed runs and a matching criterion.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant double-descent results were reported. The recorded aggregate findings are the text-stated comparisons; individual curve points and additional appendix tables were not transcribed because they do not test a claim version.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep spanning an interpolation threshold. Width down-scaling runs only downward from standard widths, with no peak located.
Extended dense training curves (Fig. 6) are not analysed for epoch-wise fall-rise-fall behaviour.
Training-set size is not varied near an interpolation threshold. Subset experiments exclude chosen examples rather than sweep n.
Only deep image classifiers are used. Risk past an interpolation point across model classes is not examined.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak location.
Label noise is injected, but the study does not test whether it creates or moves a double-descent peak. It does not test multiple descents or whether tuned regularization removes a peak.
Complexity is not recounted with an effective number of parameters.

record.verdict_notes: Double descent appears only as background in the introduction. Figures plotting test error against weights remaining (Figs. 7, 11, 12) could look like model-wise curves, but they cover only down-scaling from standard widths, under pruning or noise. They do not identify the interpolation threshold the versions require. No verdict labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test a fall-rise-fall curve in model size or locate a peak near the size that just fits the training set.
Does not test whether test error over epochs follows a fall-rise-fall curve.
Does not vary the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
Does not test double descent across model classes or establish behavior past an interpolation point.
Does not predict peak locations using a single effective-complexity measure.

Although it injects label noise and studies pruning's regularization effects, it does not test whether noise drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
Does not recount complexity using an effective parameter measure or test whether this makes a second descent an ordinary U-shape.

rows.subject: LeNet, ResNet20, VGG-16, ResNet32, and ResNet50 benchmark aggregate
rows.size_stated: varied sparsity; numerical sizes not stated for this aggregate
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error across pruning sparsities and selected the model with the best validation error.

conditions.value: random label noise; levels varied by benchmark

rows.measure: Test error at optimal sparsity relative to the dense model
rows.value: Better on 11 out of 13 benchmarks; matches on the other benchmarks.
rows.note: This is a reported pruning outcome at selected optimal sparsities, not evidence about a double-descent shape or interpolation threshold.

rows.subject: LeNet, ResNet20, VGG-16, ResNet32, and ResNet50 benchmark aggregate
rows.operation_detail: Trained dense models for pruning-equivalent steps using the cyclic learning-rate schedule.
rows.baseline: Optimally sparse model produced by pruning
rows.value: Extended dense training matches or exceeds the optimally sparse model's generalization.
rows.note: The reported result concerns the comparison with pruning, not an epoch-wise double-descent test.

rows.subject: LeNet, ResNet20, VGG-16, ResNet32, and ResNet50 benchmark aggregate
rows.size_stated: dense models with width reduced successively; each next model has 80% of the prior model's width
rows.operation_detail: Compared width-down-scaled dense models with pruned models.
rows.value: Width down-scaling under-performs pruning on 4 out of 5 benchmarks.
rows.note: This is a comparison of two size-reduction procedures; it does not report the claimed double-descent pattern.

rows.subject: LeNet, ResNet20, VGG-16, ResNet32, and ResNet50 benchmark aggregate
rows.size_stated: dense models with width reduced successively; each next model has 80% of the prior model's width
rows.operation_detail: Compared width-down-scaled dense models with pruned models.
rows.value: Width down-scaling has similar regularization effects; the gap in minimum test error between width-down-scaled and pruned models ranges from matching to 2.1% across the reported benchmarks.
rows.note: The reported comparison concerns noisy-data generalization and model-size reduction, not a double-descent curve.
rows.check: The value says the pruning-minus-width gap runs 'from matching to 2.1%', but omits LeNet. There, per Section 5.2, the gap is -4 to 0.4%: pruning does worse than width down-scaling by up to 4%. The 'no worse by more than 2.1%' figure is the authors' summary bound for width down-scaling versus pruning. The row should state the per-architecture ranges.

rows.subject: LeNet, ResNet20, VGG-16, ResNet32, and ResNet50 benchmark aggregate
rows.operation_detail: Compared extended dense training with pruning over training epochs.

conditions.value: present; 13 benchmark settings across architectures and noise levels

rows.value: Extended dense training underperforms pruning on 9 out of the 13 benchmarks; the reported differences range from 0 (matching) to 2.6%, 0.4 to 14.5%, 3.6 to 34.2%, 0 (matching) to 4.8%, and -0.3% for LeNet, ResNet20, VGG-16, ResNet32, and ResNet50, respectively.
rows.note: The epoch sweep compares extended dense training with pruning. It does not state or test an epoch-wise fall-rise-fall curve.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
